newsitem.title: POLAND: Kissinger vows to work for NATO enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Kissinger vows to work for NATO enlargement.

text.p: U.S. elder statesman Henry Kissinger told Poles on Friday he fully supported their inclusion in NATO and would cancel all appointments to help persuade the U.S. Senate to ratify it.

"I have told the President (Bill Clinton) and the Secretary of State that they can count on me to support ratification," said Kissinger, who was national security adviser and secretary of state under presidents Nixon and Ford.

"They can schedule me for hearings without having to check my schedule, because I give it priority," the veteran foreign policy guru, who was decorated this week by Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski, told a news conference in Warsaw.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic expect to be invited at next week's NATO summit in Madrid to start talks on joining the alliance -- a move that has been championed by Clinton.

But their entry, targeted for 1999, will have to be ratified by legislators of all 16 member countries, and most crucially by at least 67 of the 100 U.S. senators in a vote likely to fall in the second half of next year.

Poland fears the Senate vote could be very close and its anxieties were fuelled by a letter to Clinton last week from 46 ex-senators and other influential voices of the U.S. foreign policy establishment, opposing NATO enlargement on the ground that it could undermine the democrats now ruling in Russia.
Kissinger said that for the Senate to vote against enlargement after it had been agreed would hurt U.S. prestige.

"Even if you oppose enlargement in the abstract, to make it fail now would be such a disaster...and such a weakening of American prestige that I cannot understand how people can take that decision," he said.
Kissinger said that partly for this reason he expected that the Senate to approve inclusion of the three former Soviet bloc states in the Western defence pact.
But he said it was hard to judge as attitudes were split across Republican and Democratic party lines and probably more Republicans that Clinton's Democrats would back ratification.
"I think it will be a tough fight, but I think it can be won," said Kissinger, adding that while he often criticised Clinton's foreign policy, on NATO enlargement he backed it.

But he did criticise a charter concluded earlier this year between NATO and Russia, paving the way for enlargement, saying Moscow's participation in creating a European security order should have been secured in some other forum.
"The Russians will try to discourage ratification to the greatest extent possible by briefing a lot of people on how much it represents a threat to them," said Kissinger.
He said many Russians hoped to reintegrate Ukraine and one of Russia's aims was to try to reconstruct its former empire.
"I think this would be a historic mistake," he said, adding that it would lead to a revival of tensions and conflicts which had been a disaster this century.
Clinton plans to visit Poland on July 10, straight from Madrid, and address many thousands of Poles who will be celebrating the NATO invitation on a Warsaw square.

U.S. ambassador Nicholas Rey earlier told reporters that via television the event would help drive home to U.S. public opinion how committed the three new candidates were to NATO and to bearing their share of the financial and other burdens.
"Americans will be able to see how very important to Poles, to the whole nation, this invitation to NATO is," said Rey.
